The order required individuals and businesses to deliver their gold holdings to the Federal Reserve in exchange for an equivalent amount of paper currency at a fixed price of $20.67 per ounce of gold.

As people hoarded gold and the money supply contracted, deflation set in, leading to falling prices, reduced spending, and a worsening economic situation.

By confiscating gold, the government aimed to increase the money supply, thereby easing deflation and stimulating economic growth. After the gold was collected, the Gold Reserve Act of 1934 raised the official price of gold from $20.67 to $35 per ounce, effectively devaluing the dollar and increasing the money supply. This move was a part of a broader set of policies known as the New Deal, which aimed to help the U.S. recover from the Great Depression.

The Emancipation Proclamation, issued by President Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, declared that all slaves in the Confederate states "shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free." This proclamation did not immediately free all slaves as it only applied to Confederate states. However, the proclamation made the ending of slavery a central goal of the Civil War and gave the Union army the right to free any slaves they encountered while in Confederate territory. 

The Emancipation Proclamation was significant in the abolition of slavery because it marked a fundamental shift in the Union's war aims. Prior to the proclamation, the Union had focused on restoring the unity of the country rather than ending slavery. By declaring slavery illegal, it helped end the Confederacy's efforts to gain foreign recognition and support, especially from European powers, who had already abolished slavery. The proclamation thus helped preserve the Union and brought the U.S closer to its European counterparts. 

Finally, the Emancipation Proclamation paved the way for the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, which formally abolished slavery throughout the United States on December 6, 1865. While it took more than two years after the proclamation for slavery to be completely abolished, the Emancipation Proclamation was a crucial step towards that ultimate goal.
